structure.title: Living well and becoming good
structure.text: Early books ask what human flourishing involves and how habits, choice, and responsibility shape character.

structure.title: Judgment, friendship, and pleasure
structure.text: Later books examine practical intelligence, weakness of will, friendship, and the activities that could complete a good life.

people.name: Flourishing
people.text: Aristotle's answer to what we are all ultimately aiming at: living well and doing well, over a whole life, not just feeling good.

people.name: Virtue
people.text: A settled habit of acting and feeling rightly, learned by practice, like courage or generosity, often lying between two extremes.

people.name: Practical wisdom
people.text: The ability to see what a particular situation calls for and act on it, which Aristotle thinks no rulebook can replace.

context.title: Happiness as a life
context.text: The central term concerns flourishing rather than a passing pleasant feeling. A whole pattern of activity matters to the assessment.
context.takeaway: Pleasure alone does not settle the question.

context.title: The mean
context.text: Virtue finds an appropriate response between failures of excess and deficiency. This is not a rule to split every difference numerically.

notice.text: Notice the role of pleasure in habit.
notice.why: What someone enjoys reveals how deeply a disposition is formed.
Flourishing depends on shared activities and recognition.

opening: Someone can have money, admiration, and every pleasure available, and still have lived badly. Aristotle wants an account of a good life that can explain why. He examines the choices that become habits, the friends who shape judgment, and the uncomfortable gap between knowing what to do and doing it. His subject is the life a person actually practises over years, including what they enjoy, what makes them angry, and whether their apparent success has left them capable of using it well.
